summary: With the use of sound and language, we make the NASA visual experience more exhilarating and understandable to all. EcoSonic is a website with a user-friendly interface  designed to address the challenge of the accessibility of NASA’s visual data, specifically Normalized Difference Vegetative Index (NDVI) visuals, to people who have challenges understanding  the complex nature of them.  Through the use of  pitch variants, tempos and tone, we help one not only see but hear the changes that are occurring in the world around us. As the world is full of people of different tongues, we give everyone the chance to explore the data in the language easiest to them. And with the help of our trusted interactive tool, we allow one to navigate the website by just speaking to it. The website can be used as a teaching aid in schools for children, by students in higher education institutions, by environmental decision makers to understand the change in the variables and by any curious earth explorer who wants to understand the variable of NDVI more. Therefore, it is  built to act as a bridge to leave no one behind in understanding our changing world.
details:
Project details

EcoSonic is a website capitalising on the use of Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), which is a remote-sensing metric used to quantify the greenness, density, and health of vegetation. Specifically: 

  • Explore Earth: Users interact with a 3D globe and select places anywhere in the world.
  • Explore vegetation: It displays vegetation information using NASA satellite imagery and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI).
  • Understand vegetation conditions: It provides an indication of how much vegetation is present in a selected area. 
  • Listen to the data: It converts the vegetation reading into sound, allowing users to hear differences between locations.
  • Learn about the planet: It provides explanations, satellite imagery and a 12-month vegetation animation to help users understand changes over time.

How it works:

Stage 1: The user selects a location

The user clicks on the 3D globe or searches for a place, such as Lusaka, the Amazon Rainforest or the Congo Basin.

 

 2: The model retrieves satellite imagery

The application requests imagery from NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS). It uses the MODIS Terra 8-day NDVI layer to explore vegetation conditions, alongside true-colour imagery for visual context.

Stage 3: It estimates the vegetation reading

The model examines the NDVI image around the selected location. In the current implementation, it estimates the NDVI by matching the image colours to a colour reference table. It averages a small 5 × 5 pixel area to produce a reading.

NDVI is based on the relationship between red and near-infrared light:

NDVI=NIR-RedNIR+Red

Stage 4: The reading becomes sound

This is the most distinctive part of your project: the model uses the NDVI reading to control musical characteristics.

Sonification:

Sonification refers to the translation of imagery or videos into sound. The project incorporates this feature  as a subsidiary to NDVI satellite images and videos. The relevance of sonification to the project is to widen the inclusion of different various social groups of society. Subsequently, it provides assistance to those unable to interpret numerical data by generating sounds of different pitches as well as making it easier to understand how NDVI varies overtime.

  • Higher NDVI → higher musical pitch.

                     → more notes.

                     → faster rhythm.

                     →brighter and fuller sound.

Lower vegetation readings produce fewer, slower and softer notes.

Accessibility and Impact.

  • There are several groups that could benefit from blend and variation in the scientific data presented such as climate scientists, forest managers, conservationists, carbon market regulators, and disaster response agencies 
  • Measuring the 3D vertical structure of plants and trees allows these groups to accurately calculate stored carbon, monitor biodiversity, and predict environmental hazards.
  • People who are interested and are visually impaired could use the interactive setting to hear the variations in the variable at hand to understand what's before them, bringing it to a form beneficial to them.
  • Easy to use therefore making the information accessible to young children.

Limitation and future improvements

Our prototype is mainly based on sonification of images (changing visual information to audio information) that are on earth vegetation images based on height.

  •  It does not deal with any other variables at the moment therefore it can be improved to include other factors such as temperature to make it more impactful.
  • It does not yet cater for other impairments people may have. 
  • It relies heavily on internet access as it directly feeds from NASA data
